title: How to Install a Dryer Vent the Right Way
h1: How Do You Install a Dryer Vent Safely and Correctly?
description: A dryer vent that is installed right dries clothes faster and lowers fire risk. Learn the materials, routing rules and steps for a safe dryer vent setup.
quick_answer: Use rigid or semi-rigid metal duct, keep the run as short and straight as possible, connect sections with foil tape instead of screws, and end at an exterior hood with a damper. Follow your dryer's installation manual for maximum length. Never vent into an attic, crawl space or garage, and never use plastic or foil accordion duct.
body:
A dryer vent looks simple, just a tube from the back of the dryer to the outside. But how it's installed decides how fast your clothes dry, how hard the dryer works, and how much lint builds up inside. A poor install also lets lint pile up faster, and lint buildup is behind a lot of dryer fires.

What materials should you use for a dryer vent?

  • Rigid metal duct for the main run. It has smooth walls that don't trap lint. Four inches in diameter is standard.
  • Semi-rigid aluminum duct for the short connector between the dryer and the wall. It bends without crushing as easily as foil.
  • Aluminum foil tape to seal joints. Not cloth duct tape, which dries out and falls off.
  • An exterior vent hood with a damper or flap that closes when the dryer is off.
  • Clamps to hold the connector to the dryer and wall outlet.

Skip white vinyl or plastic duct and thin foil accordion duct. They sag, crush and trap lint in their ridges, and plastic duct is a fire hazard.

How long can a dryer vent be?

Check your dryer's installation manual first. It lists the maximum length the manufacturer allows. Building codes also set a limit, and each elbow counts as extra length because it slows the air. As a general rule, the shorter and straighter the run, the better.

That's a challenge in many Southern California homes, where laundry sits in an interior closet or hallway and the vent has to travel through the attic to the roof. Long runs work, but they need to be planned carefully and cleaned more often. Some need a booster fan made for dryer exhaust.

What are the steps to install a dryer vent?

  1. Plan the route. Pick the shortest path to an exterior wall or roof, with as few turns as possible.
  2. Cut the exterior opening if there isn't one, sized for a 4-inch duct. Seal around the hood with exterior caulk.
  3. Install the rigid duct from the wall outlet to the exterior hood. Point the male end of each section toward the outside so lint doesn't catch on the seams.
  4. Seal the joints with foil tape. Don't use screws through the duct, because they snag lint.
  5. Support the duct with straps every few feet in attics or walls so it doesn't sag.
  6. Connect the dryer with a short semi-rigid connector and clamps, leaving room to push the dryer back without crushing it.
  7. Test it. Run the dryer and go outside. You should feel strong, warm airflow and see the damper open.

Where should a dryer vent never go?

  • Into the attic, crawl space or between walls
  • Into the garage or under the house
  • Through a window screen or under a deck where lint collects
  • Into a chimney or plumbing vent

Dumping dryer exhaust indoors puts moisture and lint where it can cause mold and fires. Indoor lint traps sold for electric dryers don't solve this either. They still release humid air and fine lint into the room. We find attic-vented dryers fairly often in older homes, and it's worth fixing right away.

Gas dryers add another reason to get it right: the exhaust carries combustion gases, including carbon monoxide. If anyone in the house feels dizzy, nauseous or has a headache that clears when they leave, get everyone out and call 911.

How do you keep a new dryer vent working well?

Even a perfect install collects lint over time. Clean the lint screen after every load, and wash it with soap and water every few months if you use dryer sheets, which leave a film that blocks airflow. Check the outside hood every few months to make sure the damper opens freely and nothing is nesting in it. Most homes should have the full vent line cleaned about once a year. Large families, homes with pets, and long or roof-mounted runs often need it more often.

When is it better to hire a pro?

A straight run through an exterior wall is a reasonable weekend project. Roof vents, long attic runs, second-floor laundry rooms and any work near a gas line are better left to a professional. Our dryer vent team installs, repairs and reroutes vents, and we check the airflow at the hood before we leave.
faqs: Can I use flexible foil duct for my dryer vent?
Only as a short connector, and semi-rigid aluminum is better. The main run should be rigid metal. Foil accordion duct crushes easily and its ridges trap lint, which raises fire risk.
Can a dryer vent go through the roof?

Yes, and many San Diego and Orange County homes vent this way. Use a roof cap designed for dryer exhaust, not a standard roof vent, and plan on cleaning it more often because lint has to travel farther and uphill.
Should I use screws to connect dryer vent sections?
No. Screws stick into the airflow and catch lint. Use foil tape on each joint, with clamps only where the duct connects to the dryer and wall outlet.
How do I know if my dryer vent is installed wrong?
Long drying times, a hot laundry room, a burning smell, lint around the dryer or a damper that barely opens outside all point to an installation or blockage problem.
What Size Is a Dryer Vent? Standard Dimensions Explained?

Standard residential dryer vents are 4 inches in diameter. That's the size most dryers are built for and the size the code is built around. The vent should be smooth metal duct, with a short metal transition hose behind the dryer. Don't reduce it to a smaller size, and don't assume a bigger duct will work better.
Where Does a Dryer Vent Go? Where It Should Exit Your House?

A dryer vent should run from the back of the dryer to the outside of the house and end at a proper vent cap, usually on an exterior wall or the roof. It should never end in the attic, garage, crawl space or inside a wall. Shorter, straighter runs with smooth metal duct work best.
